title: Mini executor protocol and SDK UX playbook
content:
Context
This is a working PRD-style playbook exploring a minimal "mini-executor" protocol for the Hosted API streaming surface. The goal is pragmatic: give SDKs a small, predictable primitive that supports low-latency partials, explicit tool invocation, and structured output checkpoints while keeping client-side ergonomics simple.

Why this problem now
- Growing number of clients want finer control over when model output becomes "actionable" (e.g., call external APIs, write to DB) without coupling to long, brittle full-response parsing.
- Many streaming patterns we've prototyped are either heavyweight (many frames + state) or leaky for clients that just need simple semantics.
- We want one stable, minimal primitive that: supports incremental fidelity, clearly delineates tool-call boundaries, and keeps telemetry and replayability straightforward.

High-level concept: mini-executor
The mini-executor is a compact frame protocol layered on top of our streaming channel. It exposes two primary concepts to client SDKs and servers:
- executor-frame: a compact, atomic unit representing either partial content, a structured action proposal (tool call), or a commit/abort checkpoint.
- lease-token: a short opaque token the client obtains to execute or accept a tool call outcome (used for idempotency, local retries, and secure actuation).

Core semantics (developer-facing)
- Incremental partials: text fragments can be emitted as normal partials with a stable sequence id. Each partial is tentatively draft; clients should treat them as "display-only" until a subsequent commit frame arrives.
- Action proposals: when model decides to call a tool, it emits a proposal executor-frame with a compact typed payload (tool id, args JSON blob, confidence, optional schema pointer). The SDK surface provides a developer callback to either auto-accept, validate, or surface to the app for manual confirmation.
- Commit checkpoint: a commit frame marks a boundary where prior partials and any accepted proposals become durable for replay and billing semantics (commit id included). Commit frames are the only frames that can be used as canonical resume points for session recovery.
- Abort/rollback: if the model or server emits an abort frame for a specific commit id, clients should discard uncommitted local actions tied to that commit id.

API ergonomics (SDK patterns)
- Minimal callback set: onPartial(partialText, meta), onProposal(proposal, leaseToken), onCommit(commitId), onAbort(commitId).
- Default policies: SDKs ship with two default policies: "display-only" (partial render, auto-defer tool execution until commit) and "optimistic-actuate" (auto-execute proposals immediately but buffer downstream effects until commit).
- Lease usage: when onProposal delivers a leaseToken, the SDK can call a lightweight /execute endpoint with the leaseToken + chosen execution args. Execution returns either a result frame which will be pipelined into the stream or a failure that can be retried locally. Executions invoked before commit are tentatively visible in the client with a flagged state.
- Structured output typing: proposals and results should carry a schema_id pointer (small stable string) referencing a schema stored in the model catalog. SDKs can optionally fetch schema descriptions for validation and editor hints.

Frame shapes (compact text notation)
- PARTIAL: [{seq}]: "...text"
- PROPOSE: [{seq}][PROPOSE][tool:search][args_schema:v1][lease:lt_abc123] {"q":"weather sf"}
- EXECUTE-ACK: [lease:lt_abc123][EXEC-OK] {"result_id":"r_9"}
- RESULT: [seq][RESULT][r_9] {"items": [...] }
- COMMIT: [commit:c_42][seq_to:120][safe_ts:2025-03-28T12:30:45Z]
- ABORT: [commit:c_42][ABORT][reason:"uncertain_generation"]

Operational considerations
- Idempotency and replay: lease-token + commit id give us a two-key model for safe retries. Execution calls are idempotent by lease; commit is the canonical signal to persist results. This keeps server-side bookkeeping tractable.
- Cost accounting: billing should attribute tokens to the session once associated commit is emitted; previous partial tokens can be marked as provisional and not billed until commit threshold or a configurable grace window. Policy decision required (see open questions).
- Latency budgets: streaming transport remains optimized for small frames; PROPOSE frames must be <2 KB in the common case (tool name, small args). For large argument blobs, prefer upload-by-reference and include a short ref token in the frame.
- Failure modes: network partition before commit: when client reconnects, resume at last known commit id. Any in-flight leases prior to that commit are considered orphaned and should be garbage-collected after a short TTL.

Security and safety
- Least-privilege lease tokens: lease tokens are short-lived and scoped to a session; SDKs must not persist them beyond session lifetime. Servers validate token origin before allowing execute calls.
- Tool gating: proposals include confidence score and optional safety hints. The policy layer (either server or tenant config) can downgrade proposals into manual-review decisions.

Developer-first UX scenarios
1) Chat UI with inline actions (auto-accept off): partials render as typing. When a proposal arrives for "create-calendar-event", the UI shows a confirmation card (populated using args schema). The user confirms; SDK calls /execute with leaseToken. Once server emits commit, calendar event is finalized and the commit id is associated with the saved object.
2) Background summarizer (optimistic-actuate): app chooses optimistic-actuate. Proposals for external summarization are executed immediately; summaries are shown in app but flagged as provisional. On commit, app flips items to confirmed and updates analytics. If abort received, app rolls back the change and surfaces a retry option.

Telemetry and observability
- Required telemetry points: proposal_emitted, execute_called (with result code), commit_received, abort_received, lease-expired. Each event should surface minimal identifiers (session id, commit id, lease id) and anonymized latency and token counts.
- SLOs to measure: median proposal-to-execute latency, 95th execute-to-result latency, commit-stability window (time between proposal and commit) and rate of orphaned leases.

Testing & rollout plan
- Phase 0 (internal dogfood): add primitive to experimental SDKs behind feature flag. Test with 3 internal apps (chat playground, scheduled task runner, ticket summarizer).
- Phase 1 (beta): surface to early customers as opt-in. Collect telemetry, tighten idempotency semantics, and validate cost-accounting tradeoffs.
- Phase 2 (GA): promote to default streaming contract with clear migration docs and SDKs updated to provide default policies.

Open decisions and trade-offs
- Billing policy: bill at commit vs bill incremental but credit back aborts. Trade-off: customer predictability vs platform revenue smoothing.
- Commit cadence: should we allow client-driven commits (SDK triggers commit) vs server-emitted commits only? Client-triggered commits can speed durability but complicate authorization.
- Schema hosting: central schema registry (model-catalog-backed) vs piggyback schemas in frames. Registry reduces payload size but adds lookup latency.

Implementation notes (server side)
- Minimal state machine per session: {last_commit, pending_leases: map[lease]->meta, seq_cursor}. Garbage-collect leases after TTL (configurable).
- Storage: commits append to session log; commit checkpoint contains pointers to any executed results (result ids) and a compact summary for quick resume.
- Backpressure: if server CPU or model queue backs up, it can throttle proposal emission (returning a throttle hint frame) to signal SDKs to switch to a conservative policy.

Developer docs quickstart (SDK pseudo-API)
- connect(sessionOpts) -> session
- session.onPartial(fn)
- session.onProposal(fn(proposal, lease) => { accept|defer|reject })
- session.executeLease(lease, execArgs) -> promise(result)
- session.onCommit(fn(commitId))
- session.resumeFrom(commitId) -> session

Appendix: short example transcript
[client connects]
PARTIAL[1]: "I found some possible matches for flights to SFO..."
PROPOSE[2][tool:book-flight][lease:lt_A1]{"itinerary":{"from":"SFO","to":"JFK","date":"2025-05-02"}}
(onProposal -> SDK surfaces confirmation card)
CLIENT -> /execute {lease:lt_A1, payment_method:"pm_99"}
EXEC-ACK[lt_A1][EXEC-OK]{"booking_ref":"bk_475"}
RESULT[3][r_475]{"status":"pending_confirmation","booking_ref":"bk_475"}
COMMIT[c_7][seq_to:3]

Summary
The mini-executor aims to be a small, practical contract: compact frames, explicit proposal/execute/commit semantics, and an SDK surface that minimizes developer cognitive load while enabling safe tool actuation. This playbook is a draft — main objectives are to validate idempotency via lease tokens, refine billing commit semantics, and prototype SDK default policies to reduce integration complexity for customers.

Next steps
- Engineering: prototype server state machine and lease token lifecycle (owner: Liam Chen)
- SDK: implement experimental callbacks and default policies in JS/Go SDKs (owner: Aisha Rao)
- Product: finalize billing recommendation for beta (owner: Noah Alvarez)

Notes to reviewers
- Focus feedback on: commit/billing trade-offs, whether lease-token lifecycle is acceptable for enterprise security, and SDK default policies that feel safe for newcomers.
